1222-cobb-s-anatomy:
Irvin S. Cobb, a Kentucky humorist famed for his newspaper columns, turns his comic eye on the human body in this book. Chapters on tummies, teeth, hair, hands, and feet mix tall tales, doctor jokes, and mock science, all in Cobb's easy, drawling voice.

The humor is homely and old-style: fat men and their vests, dentists and their drills, and the trials of getting old. Cobb never aims high, but his jokes land with warmth. The book suits readers who like gentle American humor and a laugh at the body's frailties.
12417-fishin-jimmy:
Annie Trumbull Slosson's 1889 story opens at Franconia, a peaceful village among New Hampshire hills, on the margin of Pond Brook behind Uncle Eben's. Boys tempt trout with fly or worm while the narrator roams for spring flowers and butterflies, until a voice cries Strike him, sonny, and an old man steps noiselessly through the bushes.

That man is Fishin' Jimmy, spare, wiry, stooped, with a thin brown face, a local angler and storyteller. Slosson lets Jimmy's talk, humour and country wisdom carry a gentle tale of village life and nature. The book is a small, warm sketch, valued for its dialect voice and its affection for New Hampshire streams and summers.
13020-the-boy-allies-at-verdun-or-saving:
Clair W. Hayes set The Boy Allies at Verdun in February 1916, on the eve of the war's most bitter battle to that date. An automobile speeds north along a French line held for nearly two years, carrying a youth of eighteen in a British lieutenant's uniform and two companions. German armies press toward the heart of France.

A night infiltration scene finds Hal and Chester watching German troopers dig breastworks, wandering among them, then sprinting for trees at Hal's whispered word. Hayes keeps the action close and fast. Young readers got here a vivid Verdun tale from the war's own years.
15636-the-future-of-astronomy:
Edward C. Pickering, of Harvard College Observatory, wrote this essay on the future of star study, reprinted from Popular Science Monthly of August 1909. Pickering claims star study is not only the oldest science but the most advanced, since no other science has had such backing from kings, the state, and rich givers. Recent years, he notes, gave star watchers larger jobs than any other branch of pure science.

Physics, Pickering admits, pays better in use: the phone, power sent by wire, wireless, and the sea cable all grew from deep rules, with huge cash gains. Yet few labs for pure study exist, except those paid for by the state. Star study, by contrast, commands fine scopes, tools, and gifts. Pickering looks ahead to bigger scopes, sky maps, and lists, and to a science growing by big, planned work.
15644-thirteen-months-in-the-rebel-army:
William G. Stevenson, an impressed New Yorker, published this Civil War narrative in New York in 1862, with A. S. Barnes and Burr. The subtitle promises personal adventures in the infantry, ordnance, cavalry, courier, and hospital services, with an exhibition of the power, purposes, earnestness, military despotism, and demoralization of the South. A frontispiece shows a council of war before Pittsburg Landing.

Chapter one tells how Stevenson volunteered, went to Arkansas, faced questions on slavery, and met Judge Lynch at midnight. Butler Cavins and his lariat, an acquittal, and an attempted escape follow. Later chapters trace his service across the rebel army's branches, ending in hospital work. The book is a rare insider account: a Northern man trapped in Southern uniform, watching the Confederacy from inside its ranks.
15962-essays-on-political-economy:
A set of essays on political economy by Frederic Bastiat, member of the Institute of France, in the third People's Edition. G. P. Putnam's Sons issued it in New York in 1874, with a London printing by Provost and Company. Bastiat, a French liberal, argues for free trade and limited government in plain, witty prose. His essays made him famous across Europe.

Capital and Interest opens with a sack of corn, a house, and a plane, showing how capital earns its return. That Which Is Seen, and That Which Is Not Seen, follows, with the broken window, disbanding troops, taxes, theatres, and public works. Machinery, credit, Algeria, and frugality and luxury close the lesson. Bastiat's book still teaches economics by parable: look past the seen gain to the unseen cost.
16078-the-amateur-army:
Patrick MacGill's 1915 memoir tells how a working man joined Kitchener's Army and learned to be a soldier. Chapters run from enlisting and billeting through rations and sick parade, pickets and special leave, officers and rifles, the coffee shop, and the night side of soldiering. Divisional exercise, mimic warfare, a general's inspection, and endless waiting lead at last to the battalion moving off.

MacGill, author of Children of the Dead End, writes in a plain, wry voice about army routine, boredom, and comradeship. His book is not a battle history but a recruit's-eye view of training in wartime Britain. Readers of First World War memoirs will find it honest, funny, and human.
16227-the-uses-of-astronomy:
Edward Everett delivered this oration at Albany on August 28, 1856, for the inauguration of the Dudley Astronomical Observatory. Published in New York by Ross and Tousey, the volume adds a condensed report of the proceedings and an account of dedicating New York State Geological Hall. Everett argues the uses of astronomy for science, navigation, farming, and the wider life of a republic.

The explanatory note hopes the record will spread as fast as the newspaper editions sold out, for the good of science. Everett's eloquence, famous in his day, turns telescopes and stars into civic pride. Readers of American science history will find a stately, hopeful document from the age of observatory building.
16750-the-colored-regulars-in-the-united:
Chaplain T. G. Steward of the Twenty-fifth U.S. Infantry wrote this 1904 history of Black regulars in the United States Army, issued by the A. M. E. Book Concern in Philadelphia. A letter from Lieutenant-General Nelson A. Miles opens the book. It sketches Black American history and Black service in war from the Revolution through 1899, with chapters on the Revolution, 1812, the Civil War, and the Black regulars.

Steward writes to record service long slighted, with care for units, battles, and social roots. His tone is proud and factual, aimed at readers who want the full army story. The book remains a key early history of Black soldiers, valued for its scope and for its first-hand military voice.
18579-taken-by-the-enemy:
Oliver Optic published this boys' naval novel at Boston in 1888, first in his Blue and Gray Afloat series. It follows Captain Horatio Passford and his son Christy aboard the steam yacht Bellevite, with news from shore, a brother in the South, and a mission toward Mobile Bay. Chapters trace the Bellevite past Fort Morgan, a prisoner taken, a rebellion in the pilot house, and a cannon ball through the Leopard.

Christy matures a scheme, finds himself a prisoner, and helps run the gantlet in the closing chapters. Optic keeps the action brisk and the seamanship plain. The book is a rousing Civil War sea tale for young readers.
18800-last-enemy:
H. Beam Piper's story, from Astounding Science Fiction of August 1950, opens at a feast where Dallona of Hadron fidgets over an experiment not yet complete. Beside her sits Garnon of Roxor, who decided long before to take a step that gives her work its test, waiting only until after the election.

At the table sit Girzon, the armed Dirzed with his scarlet winged patch, and a bearded man praising a boy sensitive now in a trance at a writing machine. The boy, a low-grade imbecile awake, once produced a message from the discarnate Assassin Sirzim. The story's blurb names its theme: a pattern of belief that makes assassination an honorable profession, and a last enemy tougher than all the rest.
1905-the-governess-or-the-little-female-:
Sarah Fielding's Governess, or The Little Female Academy, published in 1749, is one of the first novels written for girls. It opens in the north of England, where a gentlewoman undertakes the education of young ladies and discharges the trust faithfully, instructing those committed to her care in lessons and in manners.

The girls tell stories, quarrel, and learn, and the book's design is moral without being dull: each tale teaches a fault and its cure. Fielding, sister of Henry Fielding, writes with clarity and kindness. The book remains a landmark in children's literature, showing the school story taking shape a century before it became a genre.
19471-badge-of-infamy:
Lester del Rey wrote this science fiction novel of Mars, first issued in paperback in the early nineteen seventies. Feldman, an amateur pilot, crash-lands with Chris and must learn to live on a world where Earth settlers are turning, body and mind, into Martians. A strange growth spreads along nerves toward the brain.

The plot mixes survival, medicine, and politics: what the change means, who fears it, and whether becoming Martian is a disease or a new birth. Del Rey uses the puzzle to ask how far humans should go to belong on another world, and what price identity pays.
21417-forty-six-years-in-the-army:
John M. Schofield, a lieutenant-general of the United States Army, tells his own career in Forty-Six Years in the Army. The book came out in 1897 and opens with his birth at Gerry, New York, in 1831. His father was a Baptist pastor and later a home missionary in the West.

Schofield traces his path from West Point, where he knew General Winfield Scott, through long service. The contents promise chapters on training, command, and the great wars of his time. He offers the book to young citizens whose skill must guard the Union. It is a senior soldier's plain record of a full life.
22095-the-red-cross-girls-with-the-russi:
Margaret Vandercook sent her Red Cross Girls to a new front in The Red Cross Girls with the Russian Army, published in 1916. Her heroines were American girls doing war relief in Europe. In this volume, Eugenia and her friends reach the eastern war. Eugenia risks her liberty, and nearly her life, by hiding a Belgian officer and his family.

With her help the officer wins papers from the enemy and escapes back to King Albert's army. Russian hospitals, refugees, and spies fill the rest of the tale. Vandercook wrote for girl readers who followed the war in the newspapers. The series gave them heroines their own age inside the great events of 1914 to 1918.
22135-the-moral-economy:
Ralph Barton Perry, a young Harvard philosopher, published The Moral Economy in 1909. Perry opens with Bishop Butler's words on provident living. Morality, he argues with Butler, is neither mystery nor mere custom. It is the observance of the laws by which a life is well and wisely spent, like a household run with care.

Perry treats morals as an economy of interests, values, and choices. He asks how competing goods can be ordered without waste of life. The style is clear and argumentative, aimed at students. Perry later won fame as William James's biographer and editor. This early book shows the practical, Jamesian cast of his thought about value and action.
23744-ahead-of-the-army:
W. O. Stoddard published Ahead of the Army in 1903, a boys' novel of the Mexican-American War. Its chapters move from far-away guns and the race of the Goshawk through the fortune of war and a norther storm. They reach the land of the Montezumas, General Scott and his army, and the Stars and Stripes in Tenochtitlan.

Ned, the young hero, carries despatches, stands under fire, and sees a lance pointed at his bosom. Señor Carfora is trapped, mountain passes are crossed, and a revolution brews. Stoddard, who also wrote The Errand Boy of Andrew Jackson, gives young readers a march to Mexico City with drums, dust, and danger in good measure.
238-dear-enemy:
Sallie McBride, Judy's college friend, inherits a job she never wanted: running the John Grier orphan asylum. Jean Webster's Dear Enemy, told in letters, opens at Christmas when Judy and Jervis hand Sallie the home's reform. A Scotch doctor arrives as bait, and Sallie sees through the trick.

Her letters mix complaints, budgets, and growing affection for children and doctor alike. Sallie reforms diet, discipline, and daily life with humor and grit. The sequel to Daddy-Long-Legs stands on its own as a comedy of work. Webster's letters keep the story brisk and warm.
24440-surgical-anatomy:
Joseph Maclise, fellow of the Royal College of Surgeons, wrote this surgical anatomy, with sixty-eight coloured plates, published by Blanchard and Lea in Philadelphia in 1859. Maclise inscribes the work to the gentlemen with whom, as a fellow-student, he was associated at London University College. He records a debt of gratitude to Samuel Cooper and Robert Liston, distinguished professors of that institution. From them he and his fellows inherited an aspiration for the light of science.

The preface states the work's object: to present to medical students, and to practitioners far from the schools, a series of dissections. These dissections show how the chief regions of the human body lie in relation to one another. The transcriber notes that the original book's binding had disintegrated after some 140 years, while its paper, printing, and multicolor images survived in amazingly good condition. Readers get surgical anatomy, plate by plate.
24770-a-prisoner-of-morro-or-in-the-hand:
Issued in 1898 under the name Ensign Clark Fitch, a pen name used by Upton Sinclair, this boys' adventure is set in the Spanish-American War. Young naval cadet Clif Faraday chases a prize, fights boarders, and ends up a prisoner in Morro Castle at Havana, with its dungeon vaults below. Plots by the villain Ignacio and the courage of friends shape his fate.

The story moves fast from sea chases to escapes, recapture, and a bold game of bluff, closing with an appeal on behalf of humanity and the Maine's sailors. Sinclair, writing young, gives readers action, honor, and a clear view of war at sea. It remains a lively period piece from the year of the Maine.
24986-tommy:
Joseph Hocking's 1916 book, published by Hodder and Stoughton, tells the story of 'Tommy,' the British private, from the testimony of the men themselves. Hocking met Tommy before he joined the army, addressing recruiting meetings for more than six months, then followed him through training camps and to France and Flanders. He stood with him near La Bassée and Neuve Chapelle, and at Ypres in trenches within a hundred yards of German sandbags, under shell fire and machine guns.

Only a small part of the story is imagination: nearly every incident was told to Hocking by Tommy himself, though the setting is fiction. Training camp brought hard work, strict discipline, and many duties, yet good fellowship made the lads healthier in body and morals than they had been at home. The book is a tribute from a civilian who tried hard to know his subject.
26014-practical-taxidermy:
Montagu Browne, curator of the town museum at Leicester, teaches amateurs to collect, preserve, and set up natural history specimens in Practical Taxidermy, second edition, revised and enlarged. A chapter on the pictorial arrangement of museums closes the book. Browne says hundreds of letters from readers of the first edition urged the revision, with new methods in modeling and artistic taxidermy.

Directions run practical: skin a fish as told, stuff head with peat and face and fins with putty, lay the skin cut upward, and ladle dry plaster from the tail end. Sew up with care, shorten the skin to make it deep not long, and ram plaster well with a short stick. A plate shows a peregrine falcon in flight and its binding. The manual is a hands on guide to lifelike mounts.
26556-myths-and-marvels-of-astronomy:
Richard A. Proctor gathered these essays into a new edition with Longmans, Green and Company in 1896, after a career writing popular astronomy. His preface says the chief charm of astronomy for many readers lies not in wonders alone, but in lore, legends, and strange fancies from old times. He promises to avoid technical terms where he can, writing for readers outside his own branch of study.

Twelve essays follow, from astrology and the religion of the Great Pyramid to Swedenborg's visions of other worlds and suns in flames. The rings of Saturn, comets as portents, the lunar hoax, and the origin of constellation figures each get a chapter. Old myths and new marvels share the book, with paradoxes and fancies weighed against what recent astronomy had revealed.
2868-the-green-mummy:
Fergus Hume wrote The Green Mummy as a mystery that starts with lovers and a professor, then deepens into a tomb, an inquest, and a string of manuscripts. Professor Braddock's orderly life mixes scientific reading after dinner with work renewed at seven each evening. A mummy, a baronet, a sea captain, and a Spanish don and his daughter upset it. Chapters promise the unexpected twice over, and Hume keeps the promise.

Clues pile up through accusations, circumstantial evidence, confessions, and a letter that reopens the past. The mummy itself links an Egyptian tomb to an English village crime. The novel rewards readers who enjoy an old-fashioned puzzle with romance, a patient detective trail, and a solution that ties the tomb to the living.
29691-taxidermy:
Leon L. Pray wrote this short handbook for the sportsman amateur, printed in New York in MCMXVI as number 47 of the Outing Handbooks. He sets out plain, workable ways to preserve trophies taken afield with gun or rod, aimed at the beginner who loves fine detail and has a fair share of patience. The book does not try to match the long works written for men who make taxidermy their trade.

Six chapters cover tools and stuff, a bird, a small mammal, game fish and small reptiles, a Virginia deer head, and a coyote. Each gives the steps in order, from skinning and cleaning to setting up and finishing the mount. Pray's tone is that of a skilled friend at the bench, and the book still serves as a clear first guide to the craft.
30295-the-social-work-of-the-salvation-a:
Edwin Gifford Lamb, A.B., studies The Social Work of the Salvation Army. A Columbia University dissertation from New York in 1909, submitted in partial fulfilment of the requirements for the degree of Doctor of Philosophy in political science, carries it. Lamb uses social in his title to signal that, save in an auxiliary way, he does not attempt to describe the religious features of the organization. That field is kept separate for clearness and impartial study.

Commander Booth-Tucker, leader of the Army in the United States from 1896 to 1904, gives the primary division in Lamb's terms. The Army evolved from two great ideas: reaching with the gospel of salvation the masses outside ordinary church influence, and caring for their temporal as well as spiritual interests. With little authentic literature on the subject, Lamb draws primarily on personal observation, visiting Salvation Army social institutions of every description.
31333-the-disfranchisement-of-the-negro-:
John L. Love's 1899 paper for the American Negro Academy examines the legal assault on Black political rights in the American South. Love opens with a line from Edmund Burke, quoted in the text. He argues that the attack works through the forms of law rather than open force. Its aim is political subjection followed by social degradation. He denies that it answers any temporary emergency or a mere question of numbers.

Love traces the roots of this animus into the past and presents the campaign as a deliberate, desperate effort of what he calls the spirit of tyranny. The paper is a compact piece of turn-of-the-century Black political thought. It helps readers see disfranchisement not as a single law but as a system built to strip the vote and its protections.
33219-political-economy:
W. Stanley Jevons's Political Economy, in the Science Primers series and published in New York in 1880, offers a short, clear introduction to economics for general readers. Jevons, professor of political economy at University College, London, states in his preface that he tried to put the truths of political economy into plain form. His chapters run from introduction and utility, through production of wealth, division of labor, and capital, to distribution, wages, trades-unions, and cooperation.

Later chapters treat tenure of land, exchange, money, credit and banking, credit cycles, the functions of government, and taxation, giving a complete primer in sixteen short steps. Jevons writes with the precision of a logician and the clarity of a teacher. The book remains a classic introduction to classical economics, and a good first step for readers who want the foundations of the subject without a heavy textbook.
3474-jeremy:
Hugh Walpole writes a novel of boyhood about Jeremy Cole. Jeremy wakes on the morning of December 8, 1892, aware that he is eight years old for the first time in his life. The chapters follow his birthday, the family dog, a Christmas pantomime, a sea captain, family pride, religion, and a visit to a cow farm. A merry go round and a long wait for Hamlet also figure.

Walpole tells the story close to Jeremy's own view, where small events carry great weight and grown ups remain half understood. The boy is obedient and his word can be trusted, yet he tests the rules of home and school. The novel suits readers who enjoy careful, warm stories of childhood in late Victorian England.
4075-the-intrusion-of-jimmy:
A comic novel by P. G. Wodehouse, The Intrusion of Jimmy, opens in farce, as a cyclone of a man bursts into a room and shifts a footstool, a small chair, a rug, and Spike. A massive boot sends the chair whirling to the wall, the rug crumples, and Spike lands on all fours, blinking.

Jimmy, gentleman burglar turned good fellow, blunders into love, society, and crime in New York. Wodehouse keeps the pace fast and the talk bright, with crooks and debutantes trading quips. Readers who enjoy light, funny adventure will find an early Wodehouse romp, full of charm and harmless mischief.
4362-personal-memoirs-of-p-h-sheridan-ge:
Philip Henry Sheridan wrote these personal memoirs of his part in the great events of three decades, above all the American Civil War. In his preface he admits the difficulty of recounting his own share without giving his acts too much weight or writing a full history of the years. He leaves readers to judge how well he met that difficulty.

Sheridan offers a record penned by his own hand, of a fight to keep the nation whole, defend liberty, and secure equal political rights. He claims no literary merit, only the importance of the events themselves. The memoirs give a general's view of campaigns, commands, and comrades, and they remain a central source for the Union war.
5434-the-physiology-of-taste-or-transcen:
Jean Anthelme Brillat-Savarin wrote The Physiology of Taste, translated from the last Paris edition by Fayette Robinson, as a witty science of eating. The book opens with aphorisms from the professor, a dialogue with his friend, and a biography, then moves into meditations on the senses, taste, and the pleasures of the table. Anecdotes about artists and statesmen illustrate the argument.

Later sections cover pot-au-feu, fowls, game, fish, truffles, sugar, coffee, and chocolate, with recipes and reflections alongside. Brillat-Savarin treats gastronomy as a serious subject and a joyful one. Readers get a classic of food writing, learned, funny, and still quoted at dinner tables.
7076-prisoner-for-blasphemy:
George William Foote tells his story as a prisoner for blasphemy, first published in 1886 by the Progressive Publishing Company of London. A Byron line at the head holds that persecution is not refutation, nor even triumph, and that the wretched infidel may be happier in prison than the proudest assailant. The chapters run from the storm brewing and a first summons through indictment, trial at the Old Bailey, and Newgate.

Later chapters follow a second trial, the Black Maria, Holloway Gaol, prison life, Parson Plaford, and a third trial, closing with loss and gain, a long night, and daylight. Foote calls the tale strange, since only three living Englishmen knew a blasphemy prisoner's lot, and painful, since unmerited suffering shames a boasted age of freedom.
7811-the-war-romance-of-the-salvation-ar:
Evangeline Booth, commander of the Salvation Army in America, tells its war work in The War Romance of the Salvation Army, written with Grace Livingston Hill and issued in 1919. A foreword answers a generous public's call, noting the Army sought only thanks from those it helped, not wide fame.

Service is the watchword, Booth writes, and no reward equals doing the most good to the most people in the most need. Through huts, canteens, and front-line help, the book records doughnuts, coffee, comfort, and prayer for troops, and a humble service that won a nation's gratitude.
8005-the-bible-king-james-version-book-5:
Moses speaks for the last time in Deuteronomy, the fifth book of the Bible, as Israel stands on the edge of the Promised Land. The book retells the law given at Sinai, urges the people to remember their deliverance from Egypt, and sets out blessings for obedience and curses for turning away. Its name means second law, since much of it restates earlier commandments for a new generation.

Deuteronomy closes with Moses viewing the land he will not enter and passing leadership to Joshua. Its speeches shaped Jewish and Christian ideas of covenant, the agreement between God and his people. In the King James Version, the long addresses carry a solemn, farewell weight, and the book remains a foundation text for understanding Israel's faith.
8172-history-of-astronomy:
George Forbes, formerly professor of natural philosophy at Anderson's College, Glasgow, wrote this history of astronomy in two periods. Book one, the geometrical period, covers primitive astronomy and astrology, ancient Chinese and Chaldean astronomy, ancient Greek astronomy, and the reign of epicycles from Ptolemy to Copernicus. Book two, the dynamical period, follows the discovery of the true solar system through Tycho Brahe, Kepler, Galileo and the telescope, and notions of gravitation. A portrait of Newton fronts the volume.

Forbes writes for general readers, explaining how humanity moved from sky myths to mathematical law. His history is clear, well ordered, and rich in anecdote. For students of science, it remains a readable classic, and a good guide to the long road from epicycles to Newton.
8232-the-world-english-bible-web-deutero:
Deuteronomy, in the World English Bible, gives Moses' farewell words in modern English, lightly reformatted from ebible. org by Martin Ward. These are the words Moses spoke to all Israel beyond the Jordan, in the fortieth year, after striking Sihon of Heshbon and Og of Bashan. The book retells the law, recalls the wilderness journey, and warns the new generation to remember, obey, and choose life as they enter the land.

The modern version keeps Deuteronomy's sermon style, with its repeated calls to remember and to love God wholly. Its place names and journeys, from Horeb by Mount Seir to Kadesh Barnea, ground the speeches in geography. For readers meeting the book fresh, this rendering offers the second law in language that reads like spoken counsel.
8436-speculations-from-political-economy:
C. B. Clarke, a Fellow of the Royal Society, offers nine articles in Speculations from Political Economy, and his introduction warns they are speculations, by no means altogether recommendations. Nearly all were suggested by considering mere propositions of political economy, some old, some given by friends, and Clarke follows each idea where it leads.

The book suits readers who like economics as a thinking game: take a principle, push it, and see what follows. Clarke writes for educated general readers rather than specialists, and his speculations touch policy, trade, and human conduct. It is a Victorian economist's notebook, curious and candid about its own limits.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-sain: The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Saint-Remy describes an abbey founded at Reims before 590, first a little chapel to St. Christopher. It gained great renown when it acquired St. Remy's relics in 553, and gifts poured in until by the ninth century it held about 700 domains, perhaps France's richest house. Secular priests first guarded the relics, then Benedictines, and Reims' archbishops served as its abbots from 780 to 945. Charlemagne received Leo the Third there, and Abbot Theodoric's basilica, dedicated by Leo the Ninth in 1049, crowned a church rebuilt after collapse.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alchemy:
Alchemy, from Arabic and Greek roots for the art itself, was the art of turning baser metals into gold and silver. It came before modern chemistry, and the first steps of the new science grew from the work of the old alchemists. The entry traces the word to an edict of Diocletian, where the Greek term first appears, and presents alchemy as chemistry's predecessor.

Many clerics practised alchemy, and works on the subject are credited to figures such as Albertus Magnus, though his De Alchimia is of doubtful authenticity. The old literature is extensive and often hard to follow, since its terms are obscure. Modern writers have added histories of the subject. The entry serves as a compact guide to the art, its writers, and its literature.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-anatomy:
Anatomy, from a Greek word for cutting up, now means the science of the form and structure of living beings. It splits into animal and vegetable anatomy. Animal anatomy further divides into comparative study across species and special study of one animal, covering embryology and morphology, with physiological, surgical, and pathological branches beside them.

The article traces the science from its early roots in sacrifice, embalming, and Homer's terms, through Hippocrates and the Greek and Latin schools, to the medieval universities. It dwells on the long debate over dissecting human bodies. It notes the use of executed criminals' bodies at Prague and Montpellier. It profiles Renaissance figures such as Zerbi and Achillini, who mapped nerves, ear bones, and parts of the gut. Later pages follow anatomy into modern European and American schools.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-astronomy:
Astronomy, from Greek astron, star, and nemein, to distribute, is a science of prehistoric antiquity born from humanity's basic needs. It divides into two main branches, astrometry and astrophysics. The first fixes the places of heavenly bodies and the second investigates their chemical and physical nature, though that division is quite recent. Antique science stopped at fixing apparent positions on the celestial sphere.

No attempt was made to explain observed facts until Greeks slowly built a theory, finally displaced by the vast fabric of gravitational theory. Descriptive astronomy rose with the telescope, giving close scrutiny of sky dwellers, while practical astronomy gained sharpness with better optics and mechanics. The long article moves from star positions to star physics, tracing a science from naked-eye mapping to modern instruments.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bernard-lamy:
Bernard Lamy, a French Oratorian scholar, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born at Le Mans in 1640, he died at Rouen in 1715 after joining the Oratory, a congregation of secular priests, in 1658. Study at Paris and Saumur led to teaching posts at Vendôme, Juilly, Le Mans, and Angers.

At Angers his teaching, judged too Cartesian, drew attack, and the rector secured his removal in 1675. Cartesian thought means the philosophy of Descartes, built on clear reasoning from first ideas. Lamy's later writings on Scripture, rhetoric, and mechanics kept his name alive, and the entry presents a versatile mind checked by suspicion.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-blasphemy:
Blasphemy, gross irreverence toward what deserves high honour, receives a full moral entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia. From Greek words for injuring reputation, it covers in a broad sense Bacon's blasphemy against learning and Paul's being blasphemed, as well as abusive speech against peoples and persons in the Vulgate.

In the strict sense it is a sin against religion, dishonouring God as first beginning and last end. The entry divides it into direct and indirect, and into contemptuous forms, from Julian's Thou hast conquered, O Galilean, to casual curses. St. Thomas treats it as a sin against faith, since it attributes to God what is unworthy of him.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-deuteronomy:
A word-study entry on Deuteronomy, a term found in Deuteronomy 17:18 and Joshua 8:32 and the title of the Pentateuch's fifth book. It renders the Latin Deuteronomium and the Greek deuteronomion, and means copy or duplicate rather than repetition. The king, raised to his throne, must copy out the law for himself, and Joshua wrote the law upon stones.

Pseudo-Athanasius read the title as second law, given by Moses under divine command, but the common reading takes it as explanation of the law, or exhortation to keep it. Wider opening questions about the book itself are left to the article on the Pentateuch, and a short source list closes the entry.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francois-lamy:
Francois Lamy, born in 1636 at Montireau in Eure-et-Loir and dead on 11 April 1711 at Saint-Denis near Paris. He was a Maurist Benedictine writer on the spiritual life and on apologetics, the defence of faith. While fighting a duel, a book of St. Benedict's Rule in his pocket saved him from a fatal sword thrust, and seeing God's finger in the escape, he took the Benedictine habit at Saint-Remi, Reims, in 1658. After ordination he served briefly as subprior of Saint-Faron at Meaux, resigning a year later out of humility.

 An intimate friend of Bossuet and among the most famous writers of his time, he left twenty printed works. They include Evident Truth of the Christian Religion and a refutation of Spinoza's new atheism.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-infamy:
Loss of a good name, when the law itself takes it away, is the canon law topic treated here. Infamy in this sense is the lessening of a person's standing in the eyes of prudent men. It counts as an irregularity: a bar to ordination, or to using orders already received. The entry separates infamy of law, which the law attaches to certain crimes, from infamy of fact, which grows from public repute.

Publication does no wrong, the entry notes, when a court has convicted a person or when scandalous repute is common knowledge. Canon law also required some prior public opinion before a judicial inquiry could narrow onto one person. Readers get a precise account of how a damaged name became a legal fact, and what doors that fact closed in church life.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-jacques-:
Jean-Jacques Barthélemy, a French scholar of coins and letters born at Cassis in 1716 and dead in Paris in 1795. He studied with Oratorians, Jesuits, and Lazarists, giving most time to Eastern tongues. He took the tonsure without orders and lived at Aubagne, devoting himself to coins under his friend Cary of Marseilles.

In 1744 Barthélemy became secretary to Boze, keeper of medals at the King's Library, joined the Academy of Inscriptions in 1747, and succeeded Boze in 1753, nearly doubling the collection. A 1754 mission to Italy sparked his famous Voyage of Young Anacharsis in Greece, begun in 1756 and finished in 1788. It is a charming survey of Greek life, arts, thought, and history.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jerome-bellam: Jerome Bellamy of Uxenden Hall near London, who died in 1586, came from an old Catholic family known for sheltering missionaries and recusants. He sympathised warmly with Mary Queen of Scots. When the Babington plot to free Mary and kill Elizabeth was exposed, Babington and two fellow plotters hid in his house. Bellamy concealed them, was arrested with them, tried and convicted on 15 September 1586, and executed within six days.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-political-eco:
Political Economy defines economics as the social science of how people provide the material means to meet their wants. The Greek oikonomia meant household management, and political economy first meant managing the household of the state. Adam Smith in 1776 gave it two aims: a plentiful revenue for the people and enough revenue for public service, enriching both people and sovereign.

The entry then follows the science's narrowing in the early nineteenth century, when Malthus and Ricardo defined it as the science of wealth, value, or exchange. Their strictly deductive method, reasoning from a few claimed universal principles, gained precision of terms but divorced the science from the economic realities of life, a divorce later economists sought to repair.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-french-ac:
Forty immortals guarding the French language make up the body described here, founded by Cardinal Richelieu in 1635. For years learned men had met weekly at Conrart's house to talk literature, among them Godeau, Giry, and Chapelain. Through the Abbé de Boisrobert, Richelieu learned of the circle and raised it into a national institution by royal letters patent.

Three officers led it: a director to preside, a chancellor to guard archives and seal, and a perpetual secretary to prepare work and keep records. The secretary, chosen by lot for life at 6,000 francs a year, became its public voice. Dictionary, grammar, and literary judgment gave the Academy lasting sway over French letters.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-joseph:
Thomas Joseph Lamy, biblical scholar and orientalist, was born at Ohey, Belgium, in 1827 and died at Louvain in 1907. Ordained priest in 1853 after study at Floreffe and Namur, he entered Louvain University, where Beelen and Lefebvre steered him toward Scripture, Eastern languages and the Fathers. He took a doctorate in theology in 1859.

His Louvain teaching ran from 1858 to 1900, covering Hebrew, Syriac, introduction to Scripture and exegesis. He succeeded Beelen in 1875. His editions of unpublished Syriac texts stand out, above all six volumes of St. Ephraem's hymns and sermons and his edition of Bar Hebraeus. His Introductio in Sacram Scripturam ran to six editions, though his texts carry many misprints.
cobb-s-anatomy:
Irvin S Cobb divided Cobb's Anatomy into four comic essays: Tummies, Teeth, Hair, and Hands and Feet. He jokes that the preface space is for rent to any respectable advertiser, which sets the book's tone exactly. Tummies opens by quarreling with Dr Woods Hutchinson, who claims fat people are happier than other people.

Cobb demands to know whether the doctor ever unfastened vest buttons for extra chins or undressed partly to read his watch. Teeth, ears like tires, and mouths built beyond specifications get the same treatment. Cobb, a Kentucky journalist turned national humorist, writes the body as a badly planned building whose tenant complains cheerfully on every page.
dear-enemy:
Jean Webster wrote Dear Enemy, published in 1915, a sequel in letters to Daddy-Long-Legs. Sallie McBride, the lively college friend of Judy Abbott, is talked into running the John Grier Home, the orphan asylum where Judy grew up. Sallie writes home about cold pipes, dull food, unhappy children, and her war of reform against habits a century old.

Her chief foe is the asylum's dour Scottish doctor, Robin MacRae, whom she names in her letters as the Enemy. Their clash over how orphans should be fed, taught, and loved drives the tale, along with fires, adoptions, and runaways. Webster uses the fun to argue for kinder, homier care of children in institutions.
doe-osti-2571755-data-structure-alchemy: Database researcher Stratos Idreos lays out a fresh way of thinking about data structures, the building blocks that decide how software stores and retrieves information. The report argues that old categories for these structures no longer fit how modern systems actually work. Readers get a new map for designing storage that runs faster and scales better.
doe-osti-3021282-plant-design-for-a-deve: Bioeconomy plants got design-workshopped, and this DOE text covers frontier science. The pages detail the report findings. The bio folks get their data. The series was workshop. The data were bio. The science was frontier. The workshop was series.
govdocs-archive_org-the-christ-myth-titl: Arthur Drews argued in The Christ Myth, published in 1909, that Jesus never existed as a historical person. Only the title page of the work is described in the record held here. Drews, a German philosopher, claimed the Christ figure grew from older myths and cults. His book caused a public storm in Germany and still anchors the Christ myth debate. The title page alone marks that famous and fought-over work.
jeremy:
Hugh Walpole wrote Jeremy, a novel about an English boy growing up in the cathedral town of Polchester. Jeremy Cole lives in a large stone house on Orange Street with his old-fashioned family. The story opens on his eighth birthday, in December 1892. He wakes before dawn, certain that being eight changes everything. Walpole follows him through one formative stretch of childhood.

Chapters cover a family dog, a Christmas pantomime, and a formidable governess, Miss Jones. A sea-captain visitor, family pride, and questions of religion widen Jeremy's world. A trip to Cow Farm and his sister's awakening test his loyalties. The family servant Mary and a merry-go-round bring the year around. Readers get a tender, detailed portrait of a sensitive boy learning fear, faith, and love inside a strict Victorian household.
last-enemy:
H. Beam Piper's story Last Enemy first ran in Astounding Science Fiction in August 1950. A note warns that its last enemy was the toughest of all. Winning against him carried its own danger.

The tale opens at a U-shaped dinner table as talk dies down. Soft music drifts over the guests. Behind that calm sits a society shaped by strange beliefs. In that world, killing can count as an honorable profession. Piper builds science fiction from that single unsettling custom and its effects. The dinner scene's calm opening makes later dangers hit harder. Piper often built stories around one strange social rule.
personal-memoirs-of-p-h-sheridan-general:
Philip Henry Sheridan finished his Personal Memoirs in August 1888, dedicating them to his comrades in arms during the War of the Rebellion. In his preface he owns the difficulty of telling his share in great events without giving his own acts unmerited prominence. He claims no literary merit, only the importance of his subject.

The complete memoirs open with his Irish parents, who came from County Cavan to America in 1830. Sheridan tells of grocery clerking, West Point, a fistfight, suspension, and graduation. From such beginnings he rose to command the Union cavalry and become one of the war's famous generals.
pocket-lavater-physiognomy:
Two sages' face lore is shrunk for the coat in The Pocket Lavater, an English digest of near 1800. Johann Caspar Lavater's great work on the face had made face lore a craze in the West. Della Porta's old beast lore stands back of it. The digest picks the best rules, signs, and draws from both and binds them in a small, cheap book for the crowd.

A clerk could learn to read a brow, nose, or chin on his walk to work. The science was false, yet the fad was vast. The book is that fad in brief.
podcast-joerogan-QwfJIFH3WMY:
Travis Walton retells his encounter with aliens in a segment of the Joe Rogan Experience. Walton's 1975 case, in which a logging crew reported a craft and Walton vanished for five days, was made into the film Fire in the Sky. He has told the story for decades, and it has not softened.

He goes over the night in the forest, the missing days, and the storm of tests and doubts that followed. Rogan asks what he remembers clearly and what remains blank. The segment adds a fresh telling of a foundational abduction case, in the voice of the man at its center.
podcast-tuckercarlson-61rCf7INomY:
Former CIA officer Bernard Hudson joins Tucker Carlson to discuss the Las Vegas Cybertruck explosion, the New Orleans truck attack, and agency corruption. Both attacks struck around New Year's Day and raised hard questions about warning signs. Hudson reads them with an operator's eye.

Hudson gives his view of what investigators may have missed in each case. He also addresses Tulsi Gabbard's move into the intelligence leadership and what it could change. Carlson presses him on how deep the rot inside the agencies runs. Watching viewers get an insider's take on a chaotic stretch of news.
prisoner-for-blasphemy:
George William Foote told the story of his own prosecution in a book first printed in London in 1886 by the Progressive Publishing Company. Foote, a freethought writer, was charged with blasphemy and tried more than once for what he had published.

Chapters follow the summons, the indictment, and trials at the Old Bailey, then take the reader inside Newgate and Holloway Gaol. Prison life, a prison chaplain, and the gains and losses of the fight fill the closing pages. Readers get a first-hand record of a famous Victorian free-speech case.
speculations-from-political-economy:
C. B. Clarke offers nine short pieces in Speculations from Political Economy, and warns that they are guesses, by no means all plans he backs. Near all grew, he says, from weighing plain claims of the science of trade and wealth. Some are old, or came from friends; some, he thinks, are new, and many will call the new ones unpractical, that being the approved word for an idea new to them.

His heads run from the yield of labor and trade answers and strikes back, through world free trade and the ransom of the land. Making the most of our land, free trade in railways, land law reform, the leveling of taxes, and the wealth of the nation close the set. The first piece takes up the yield of labor, a point Clarke says trade writers have rated too low, on cases drawn from Edward Wilson.
taken-by-the-enemy:
Taken by the Enemy opens The Blue and the Gray series. Oliver Optic wrote the series for boys. Lee and Shepard of Boston issued it. Each volume cost a dollar and a half. The publisher's list at the front divides the series into Afloat and On Land sets.

The Afloat set runs from Taken by the Enemy through Within the Enemy's Lines, On the Blockade, and Stand by the Union to Fighting for the Right and A Victorious Union. A frontispiece caption gives three cheers for Captain Passford, the series hero. Optic wrote swift, patriotic sea and war adventures in which young Union men prove themselves under fire, and this first volume launches Passford's career.
tanakh-jps-1917-deuteronomy:
Deuteronomy, the fifth book of the Torah, appears here in the Jewish Publication Society's 1917 English version of the Holy Scriptures. The book is framed as words Moses spoke to all Israel beyond the Jordan, late in the long desert march.

Moses recalls how God spoke at Horeb and urged the people to move on and take the promised land. He dates his speech to the fortieth year, after the fall of Sihon and Og, kings east of the river. Readers get law retold as a last charge, with past mercy, fresh commands, and the land set plain before a new age group poised to enter it.
the-amateur-army: Front matter alone is present for Patrick MacGill's The Amateur Army, a London book from Herbert Jenkins dated 1915 in Roman numerals. A frontispiece names its author Rifleman Patrick MacGill, and earlier works listed are Children of the Dead End and The Rat-Pit. The contents map a new soldier's first months: enlisting and being billeted, rations and sick parade, pickets and special leave, officers and rifles, a coffee-shop, and the night side of soldiering.
the-bible-king-james-version-book-5-deut:
Deuteronomy , read in the King James Version, begins with words Moses spoke to all Israel on this side of the Jordan, in a wilderness plain facing the Red Sea. Places named include Paran, Tophel, Laban, Hazeroth, and Dizahab.

A note gives eleven days' journey from Horeb to Kadeshbarnea. In the fortieth year, in the eleventh month, Moses speaks all God commanded him, after defeating Sihon of the Amorites and Og of Bashan. On this side Jordan, in Moab, Moses begins to declare the law, recalling what God spoke at Horeb. A final address, not a new conquest, opens the book.
the-boy-allies-at-verdun-or-saving-franc:
Clair W. Hayes wrote The Boy Allies at Verdun, or Saving France from the Enemy, dated 1917. The first chapter is called The Eve of Verdun. Its date is February 22, 1916, and its hour is close to six at night.

A car speeds north along the French line, which for close to two years has held back the German hosts. For months the two sides have fought to a draw from the North Sea to the Swiss line. Now the hour nears for the start of the most harsh and wasteful fight of the war so far. At the wheel sits Hal Paine, an American youth of some eighteen years, in the dress of a British horse officer. Two riders in the back seat bounce and talk as the car leaps the rough road.
the-colored-regulars-in-the-united-state:
Chaplain T. G. Steward, D.D., of the Twenty-fifth U.S. Infantry, wrote this history of Black soldiers in the United States Army. The A.M.E. Book Concern published it at Philadelphia in 1904. An introductory letter from Lieutenant-General Nelson A. Miles, commanding the Army, stands at its front.

The full title promises a sketch of the history of the colored American, plus an account of his services in the country's wars. That account runs from the Revolutionary War to 1899. Chapter I sketches social history: the importation of the Africans, the character of the colored population in 1860, and free colored people in the South and the North. Chapter II takes up the military spirit, from early literature of Negro soldiers through the Revolution, the War of 1812, and Negro troops in the Civil War. Steward writes as both chaplain and historian of his own regiments' tradition.
the-future-of-astronomy:
Edward C. Pickering, head of the Harvard College Observatory, gave this talk on the future of astronomy in 1909, first printed in the Popular Science Monthly. He asks why star study draws such rich support.

Pickering notes that observatories hold endowments near half a million dollars a year, while physics, rich in trade uses like the telephone and cable, gets far less. He asked the wisest man he knew, who said astronomy fires the imagination. Vast distances and hard puzzles draw men who made fortunes in mills and counting rooms. Pickering then maps how star study should be run and shared in the years ahead.
the-governess-or-the-little-female-acade:
Sarah Fielding wrote The Governess. Its subtitle is Or, The Little Female Academy. Its heading is dated 1749. The tale opens in the north of England. A gentlewoman takes up the schooling of young ladies there. She teaches reading, writing, needlework, and proper behavior. Her chief aim is to improve their minds in useful knowledge.

The governess is Mrs. Teachum, a clergyman's widow. She lived nine years with her husband in full accord. The pair planned with great care the education of their two little girls. Mr. Teachum loved to improve his wife by talk. One of his constant themes was the education of children. That training, cut short by his last illness, shapes the school she now runs. Her girls are to be obedient to their elders. They are to be gentle, kind, and warm to each other.
the-green-mummy: Fergus Hume wrote The Green Mummy. Only front matter is present here. It gives the title page and a contents list of twenty-one chapters. The heads open with The Lovers and Professor Braddock. They name A Mysterious Tomb, The Unexpected, and Mystery. They name The Inquest and The Captain of The Diver. They name Mrs. Jasher's Luck and The Don and His Daughter. They name The Manuscript, A Discovery, and More Mystery. They end with A Story of the Past. No chapter text is present.
the-intrusion-of-jimmy:
P. G. Wodehouse opens this novel at the Strollers' Club. The main smoking-room has filled for half an hour. Chapter I is titled Jimmy Makes a Bet. The contents promise thirty chapters of house-party comedy. Pyramus and Thisbe come early. Mr. McEachern and Molly follow. A thief in the night appears. An exhibition performance and a move to Dreever come next. Jimmy adopts a lame dog. A marriage is arranged along the way.

Wodehouse calls the Strollers' the pleasantest club, not the grandest. A young gentleman hero moves among its members. Policemen's daughters, crooks, and earls cross his path. Later headings promise loathsome gifts and family jars. A treasure-seeker and explanations follow. Stirring times await Sir Thomas. The machinery is classic early Wodehouse. A bet starts everything. An assumed errand and a great house do the rest.
the-physiology-of-taste-or-transcendenta: Brillat Savarin's The Physiology of Taste bears the subtitle Transcendental Gastronomy. Fayette Robinson translated it from the last Paris edition. Here only the title page and contents appear, so the meditations themselves are absent. The contents list short sayings by the professor, a talk between the author and his friend, a life of the author, and a preface. Numbered meditations then start with the senses and move on to taste itself.
the-uses-of-astronomy:
Edward Everett delivered The Uses of Astronomy at Albany on August 28, 1856, for the inauguration of the Dudley Astronomical Observatory. Ross and Tousey published the oration in New York the same year. The pamphlet pairs the speech with a condensed report of the proceedings and an account of dedicating New York State Geological Hall.

An explanatory note says newspaper editions of the record were exhausted within a month. The publisher hopes wide circulation of both ceremonies will benefit the cause of science in the public mind. Everett, a distinguished statesman, is praised for investing astronomy with new beauties in one of his most brilliant compositions. Demand, not profit, is offered as the motive for reprinting.
the-war-romance-of-the-salvation-army:
Evangeline Booth, commander-in-chief of the Salvation Army in America, wrote The War Romance of the Salvation Army with Grace Livingston Hill. J. T. Lippincott copyrighted the volume in 1919. Portraits show General William Bramwell Booth and Evangeline Booth herself before the narrative begins.

Her foreword answers a generous public's insistent call for an account of the Army's work during the world conflict for liberty. Service is the watchword, she writes, and no reward equals doing the most good to the most people in the most need. The Army held itself ready as American forces gathered, entered France ahead of the Expeditionary Forces, and meant to stay until the last troops came home.
the-world-english-bible-web-deuteronomy:
Book five of the World English Bible, Deuteronomy, records words Moses spoke beyond the Jordan. Israel camps in the wilderness near Suph and Paran. The timing is precise: the fortieth year, the eleventh month. Moses speaks after defeating Kings Sihon and Og. In Moab he begins declaring the law. He recalls God's command at Horeb to move on.

The people had stayed long enough at that mountain. Their journey toward the Amorites' hill country lay ahead. Deuteronomy retells the law for a new generation. Covenant loyalty shapes every speech in it. Readers meet Moses as teacher on the border of the promised land.
thirteen-months-in-the-rebel-army: William G. Stevenson is named in brackets as author of Thirteen Months in the Rebel Army, published in New York in 1862. The subtitle calls him an impressed New Yorker, meaning a man forced into service. His narrative covers infantry, ordnance, cavalry, courier, and hospital services. The title page also promises an exhibition of the power, purposes, and military despotism of the South. A frontispiece shows a council of war before Pittsburg Landing. What is present here stops at the front pages, so Stevenson's adventures themselves do not appear.
vedas-catholic-encyclopedia-remy:
Arthur Remy wrote the Catholic Encyclopedia entry on the Vedas, the oldest scriptures of Hinduism. The encyclopedia aimed to give Catholic readers sound learning on all faiths. Remy's article treats a vast subject in compact form.

He outlines the four Vedas and their hymns, prayers, and rites. He notes their age, language, and place in Indian worship. His tone is scholarly, if dated in places. The entry shows how the Church once taught its flock about a far faith. It suits readers who compare religions and want the period view stated plainly.
